entries.summary: Jones' Q2 2026 13F reveals a 730% surge in iShares Core S&P 500 ETF (IVV), making it his top portfolio move of the quarter at 1.5% of the fund. Alongside existing large positions in TSMC, Microsoft, and Nvidia, the dramatic S&P 500 ETF accumulation signals Jones is broadly bullish on U.S. equities and positioning for direct debt monetization waves he believes will reshape global economies. His portfolio of 3,431 stocks now reflects a hedged-but-long U.S. macro stance.
key_views: 730% increase in iShares Core S&P 500 ETF (IVV) position — top Q2 portfolio move at 1.5% impact
Broad U.S. equity exposure alongside top AI names (TSMC, MSFT, NVDA, Micron)
Sees coming waves of direct debt monetization reshaping global economies and financial markets
Traditional hedges like gold have done well — letting price action guide allocation
Mixed-hedged approach: long risk assets while acknowledging macro uncertainty
trade_ideas: Long iShares Core S&P 500 ETF (IVV) — massively increased position
Long TSMC, Microsoft, Nvidia, Micron in portfolio
Gold as a hedge against debt monetization

entries.summary: Tepper's Q2 2026 13F (filed Aug 14) shows he fully exited SanDisk (SNDK) after its surge, while purchasing 7.5 million shares of American Airlines — a notable cyclical bet amid his AI-heavy book. With 77% of Appaloosa's $7.73B portfolio now tied to AI-centric companies (Nvidia, TSMC, Amazon), Tepper is consolidating around core infrastructure plays while opportunistically adding beaten-down cyclicals.

77% of portfolio in AI-centric companies: Nvidia, TSMC, Amazon as core positions

Q3 2026 13F (covering Sep 30) not due until mid-November — current activity not yet public
trade_ideas: Long American Airlines (7.5M shares added)
Core AI longs: Nvidia, TSMC, Amazon
Exited SNDK (full position sold into strength)

entries.summary: Gundlach is positioned defensively on rates, favoring BBB-rated and above bonds with selective BB high-yield exposure, while explicitly avoiding CCC-rated bank loans and the long end of the Treasury curve. He sees the 30-year yield moving to the 'mid-5s' before the September Fed meeting, believes rate cuts are difficult to justify, and prefers maturities in the two-to-seven-year range as the policy path remains uncertain. A September 8 DoubleLine webcast is expected to detail updated positioning.
key_views: Favoring BBB+ investment-grade bonds; selectively adding BB high yield
Avoiding CCC bank loans — widening spreads and rising default risks
Avoiding long-end Treasuries; prefers 2-7yr maturities
30-year Treasury yield could move to mid-5s before September FOMC
Fed more likely to raise than cut rates; rate cuts 'difficult to justify'
DoubleLine Gundlach Unlocked webcast scheduled September 8
trade_ideas: Long BBB+ investment grade bonds (2-7yr maturities)
Selective BB high yield
Short/avoid long-dated Treasuries
Avoid CCC-rated bank loans

entries.summary: Burry, who deregistered Scion Asset Management from the SEC in November 2025 and now publishes positions voluntarily on Substack, is running a concentrated AI short book. He called Palantir 'worth under $1' in August 2026 and doubled his short when the stock surged 64%, with six of seven short bets — including Nvidia, Palantir, Micron, Tesla, Caterpillar, Applied Materials, and the iShares Semiconductor ETF — currently profitable. His macro view centers on distorted asset prices from passive investment vehicles and systemic supply-chain fragility.

Short Nvidia, Palantir, Micron, Tesla, Caterpillar, Applied Materials, SMH (semi ETF)
6 of 7 short positions currently profitable
Scion deregistered from SEC Nov 2025 — positions now via voluntary Substack disclosures
Passive investment vehicles causing dangerous asset price distortions
Macro risks: supply chain fragility, systemic valuation excess
trade_ideas: Short Palantir (doubled position into strength)
Short Nvidia, Micron, Tesla
Short Caterpillar, Applied Materials

entries.summary: At the G20 meeting in Asheville (September 1), Bessent defended the Treasury's bond buyback expansion as successful, claiming the U.S. has the 'best-performing bond market among major countries' since Trump took office — even as the 10-year Treasury yield rose to its highest level in nearly 20 months amid a global bond selloff. Bessent directly pushed back on his former mentor Druckenmiller's accusation that the buyback was 'price management,' while maintaining his long-term growth thesis anchored in AI productivity and elevated capital expenditure.
key_views: Claims U.S. bond market is best-performing globally since Trump's return — rebuts Druckenmiller
10-year yield at 20-month high amid global bond selloff; 1997 Asian crisis parallels raised
Defending expanded bond buyback ($4B operations Sep 9–Nov 4) against market manipulation accusations
Long-term growth thesis: AI productivity + increased U.S. investment + elevated capex
G20 Asheville: aligned with Fed Chair Warsh on spurring economic growth
trade_ideas: Treasury bond buyback program targeting 10-30yr maturities ($4B/operation)
Policy bet: AI productivity drives long-run economic expansion

entries.summary: Ackman is building institutional infrastructure around Pershing Square's newly public vehicle, targeting 15–20% investment-grade debt leverage with rating agency conversations beginning in early September, and planning to launch Pershing Square Ventures in late 2026. On the macro, Ackman is explicitly bullish, stating 'I think we're heading into a very good place' — pointing to easing geopolitical pressures, expected rate cuts, and strong investment trends. He is also reportedly exploring a new fund specifically to bet on market complacency.

Launching Pershing Square Ventures in late 2026

Q2 2026 earnings call highlights strong performance following public listing

Investment-grade leverage at 15-20% AUM
Market complacency bet (new fund reportedly being explored)

entries.summary: Greenlight Capital was essentially flat in September (down only 10 basis points) as the S&P 500 gained 2% and the Nasdaq rose 2.68%, with gold surging 6% as Greenlight's best performer while Brighthouse Financial, Kyndryl, and ODP Corp. declined 2–3.6%. Year-to-date, Greenlight is up only 9% versus the benchmarks at roughly 21%, reflecting the persistent cost of Einhorn's low-gross, capital-preservation-first posture amid a momentum-driven market.

Low gross and net exposure — explicit capital protection stance

entries.summary: Deutsche Bank's Jim Reid frames 2026 as a 'never a dull moment' year caught between '1999 meets 1990' — an AI investment frenzy reminiscent of the dot-com boom running concurrently with Middle East oil disruptions echoing the 1990 Gulf War. Reid's baseline projects 2026 global GDP at 3.0% but sharply revises headline inflation to 3.8%, with the Fed on hold indefinitely (hawkish risks rising), the ECB forced to raise rates 50bps, and the Bank of Japan tightening faster. AI productivity gains remain 'years away,' and if AI fails to deliver, already-unsustainable debt levels will worsen materially.
key_views: '1999 meets 1990': AI boom (dot-com exuberance) + Middle East oil shock (1990 Gulf War parallel)
2026 global GDP: 3.0%; headline inflation revised sharply to 3.8%
Fed on hold indefinitely — hawkish risks rising, rate cut timing pushed further out
ECB forced to raise rates 50bps; Bank of Japan accelerating tightening pace
AI productivity gains 'years away' — if AI doesn't deliver, debt crisis materially worsens
Severe oil scenario: Brent at $150/barrel would drag Europe into outright recession
Investors should 'expect no let-up in volatility' — boom-bust narrative swings ahead
trade_ideas: Hedge oil spike risk — $86/barrel base, $150/barrel severe scenario
Avoid long-duration bonds amid sticky inflation
Watch ECB tightening spillover on European assets

entries.summary: Hartnett's latest BofA Flow Show, 'Strife Begins at Forty,' warns that U.S. debt is crossing another historic milestone and frames the September 16 FOMC meeting and a potential September 18 Bank of Japan rate hike as a 'Mission Accomplished' moment for long yields. With the 30-year Treasury yield at 5.2% (highest since June 2007) and the real 30-year at 3% (highest since November 2008), Hartnett is rotating into defensives and flagging that REITs, biotech, regional banks, and small caps quietly outperforming may signal a yield peak is emerging.

Sep 16 FOMC + Sep 18 BoJ potential hike = 'Mission Accomplished' moment for yields

REITs, biotech, regional banks, small caps quietly outperforming — yield peak signal

Anything But Bonds framework intact but yield peak thesis beginning to emerge
trade_ideas: Rotate into defensives (vs. tech/growth/AI)
Long REITs, biotech, regional banks, small caps
Short AI hyperscalers and private credit if bond plan fails
Long gold as Anything But Dollar/Bonds hedge

entries.summary: Napier is actively promoting his financial repression thesis — arguing that governments will engineer a 15- to 20-year period of structurally elevated inflation (4–5.5%) to erode debt burdens, forcing savers into government bonds in a post-WWII-style regime. Unlike the post-WWII era, today's world lacks financial borders, so capital controls would likely be necessary to prevent investors from fleeing into foreign or real assets. Napier warns that this regime will produce persistently negative real bond returns and reshape portfolio construction for decades.
key_views: 15-20 year financial repression cycle ahead: 4-5.5% structural inflation in developed world
Governments will force savers to own government bonds — post-WWII playbook repeating
Capital controls likely needed since modern world lacks financial borders of the 1940s-50s
Real returns on bonds will be persistently negative during the repression period
Financial repression is government's mechanism to manage unsustainable debt without default
Investment implication: real assets and equities outperform bonds over the cycle
trade_ideas: Short/underweight government bonds (negative real returns ahead)
Long real assets (real estate, commodities, infrastructure)
Long equities over bonds for the repression cycle duration
Monitor for capital control signals — would accelerate asset relocation

entries.summary: BCA Research's Peter Berezin has raised U.S. recession odds to 40% in his Q3 2026 Strategy Outlook, citing the Iran conflict as a geopolitical shock pushing European and Japanese recession risk to 50%. Berezin fears the market is approaching a 'Wiley E. Coyote moment' where equities run on borrowed time before an AI bubble burst coincides with the recession — a dual unwind he believes could cause stocks to fall 30%.
key_views: U.S. recession odds raised to 40% — Iran conflict is the triggering geopolitical shock
Europe and Japan recession risk at 50% from Iran-driven oil supply disruption
AI bubble risk: stocks approaching 'Wiley E. Coyote moment' — up in the air before the drop
Simultaneous AI bubble burst + recession = potential 30% equity decline
Q3 2026 Strategy Outlook flags global demand destruction from energy price shock
trade_ideas: Underweight equities — Wiley E. Coyote moment risk
Reduce AI high-multiple stocks ahead of potential bubble burst
Hedge oil/energy price spikes from Iran conflict escalation

entries.summary: Mauldin's latest Frontline Thoughts introduces a 'Prepare to Muddle Through' framework: real GDP at 1.3%, inflation just under 3%, unemployment at 4.2% — conditions defining neither recession nor robust expansion but a prolonged muddling. He frames this as the 'Bipolar Economy Part 2' where geopolitics and economics are tightly intertwined, with Trump's tariff threats on Europe (tied to Greenland ambitions) adding fresh uncertainty to already-modest growth.

Muddle Through = not recession, not boom — prolonged economic malaise
'Bipolar Economy Part 2' — geopolitics and economics tightly intertwined in 2026
Trump tariff threats on Europe (Greenland dispute) adding fresh uncertainty
Geopolitics defines and constrains economic policy choices
2026: 'emotional roller coaster' — suggests hedged, patient positioning
trade_ideas: Defensive positioning for prolonged muddling — no strong directional bet
Monitor geopolitical risk: Greenland/Europe tariff threat as new catalyst

entries.summary: In a CNBC appearance hours after Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole speech, Apollo's chief economist Torsten Slok warns that if the Fed hikes rates in September, sequential hikes are likely to follow — a significant hawkish shift from his prior view that long rates could be 'a lot lower' in six months. Slok frames Warsh's 'We have work to do' as a genuine tightening signal rather than posturing, arguing the ~60% market probability of a September hike is warranted, and that investors are underestimating how many hikes follow the first.
key_views: September Fed rate hike now likely after Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole tone — 'We have work to do' signals genuine inflation commitment, not rhetorical posturing
If Fed hikes in September, sequential hikes almost certain to follow — restart of tightening cycle, not a one-and-done correction
Breaks from prior dovish view: prior stance that long rates would be 'a lot lower' in six months is no longer the base case post-Jackson Hole
Markets pricing ~60% September hike probability is correct; consensus still underestimates how many hikes follow the first
Elevated oil prices from Iran/Hormuz disruptions add commodity-driven inflation that compounds the case for Warsh-style preemptive tightening
trade_ideas: Short intermediate Treasuries (2-5yr) as September hike materializes and signals tightening cycle restart
Underweight rate-sensitive sectors (REITs, utilities, leveraged buyout credit) if multiple hikes now the base case

He argues that bond markets should be allowed to function freely rather than be subject to government manipulation, positioning himself as a skeptic of Bessent's approach to Treasury management.

entries.summary: Howard Marks' latest Oaktree memo 'AI Hurtles Ahead' examines how AI adoption is accelerating beyond initial projections, while his March 2026 conference reflections and April private credit memo warn that rapid capital deployment has created structural vulnerabilities in direct lending tied to private equity portfolio company performance. Marks maintains his core thesis: finding mispricings requires identifying market mistakes, and current AI enthusiasm creates both genuine opportunity and significant overvaluation risk.

Market cycle requires avoiding overvalued sectors while exploiting mispricings in overlooked AI beneficiaries

Long AI-adjacent companies where prices lag adoption curve

He is simultaneously betting on a Fed rate cut as early as Q1 2027, positioning ahead of what he sees as an inevitable monetary pivot. entries.summary: Apollo's chief economist Torsten Slok argues AI's labor market impact is showing up in weaker wage growth rather than mass job displacement — a subtle but significant drag on consumer spending power. More critically, he charges that AI profits are 'being funded by investors rather than earned from customers,' comparing current hyperscaler capex to investor subsidization rather than genuine commercial traction — a dynamic that historically precedes valuation corrections in tech. Software sector headwinds are now driving repricing in PIK debt yields in BDCs.

Combination of wage pressure + consumer spending deceleration + AI capex imbalance creates a non-linear risk scenario
trade_ideas: Long duration bonds — 6-month rate view is lower from current levels
Underweight AI hyperscaler equities where capex exceeds commercial revenue justification
Monitor PIK debt in listed BDCs as leading indicator of broader credit stress

entries.summary: SocGen's Albert Edwards declares his long-running 'Ice Age' secular stagnation thesis is officially over, replaced by a new paradigm of fiscal dominance and potential double-digit inflation driven by governments unable to unwind fiscal expansion. Edwards now argues the AI 'doomsday' is not a future event — disruption is already visible in current economic and labor market data — which combined with fiscal excess creates an unprecedented macro environment that bond markets are dangerously under-pricing.

Long inflation-linked assets (TIPS, gold) as double-digit inflation risk is underpriced
Reduce exposure to AI-disrupted sectors (software services, back-office, call centers)

entries.summary: Goldman Sachs chief economist Jan Hatzius argues the US economy is 'slowing beneath the surface' — underlying trend job growth has decelerated to just 5,000 per month, the recent unemployment rate improvement reflects lower participation rather than higher employment, and consumer spending will slow as the tax refund boost fades. Crucially, Hatzius says the Fed has 'no credible path to rate hikes' despite market pricing ~2.4 hikes over the next 12 months, making Goldman's stance far more dovish than futures currently imply.

Goldman August 16 note: markets 'too hawkish' on Fed rate hike bets; economy's soft underbelly will become apparent in H2 2026
trade_ideas: Long US Treasuries — Goldman significantly more dovish than market on Fed rate path
Reduce short-duration positioning as rate hike probability overstated by futures market

Nvidia (18%) and Micron (14%) together account for 32% of S&P 500 earnings growth in 2026, with the top 10 contributors representing 65% of total index earnings, creating systemic fragility as the AI trade matures.

Rally broadening in breadth (more stocks participating) while earnings growth is not — a divergence that historically resolves via earnings disappointment
Equity market structure is 'structurally unusual' — sectoral recessions and expansions happening simultaneously, defying linear analysis
Higher yields impacting markets in August 2026 — the yield level is starting to bite and will be the key variable for H2

entries.summary: 22V Research's Jordi Visser argues that Bitcoin's recent 7-sigma weekly price move signals a major macro regime transition — the kind of statistically extreme event that marks regime breaks, not mere momentum. While Wall Street concentrates capital into AI infrastructure, Visser is buying Bitcoin as his primary hedge against an 'age of AI-driven abundance,' viewing digital scarcity as the anti-thesis trade to an AI economy that systematically compresses margins, wages, and the value of traditional services.

Wall Street consensus all-in on AI infrastructure; the contrarian macro trade is Bitcoin as abundance-era scarcity hedge

Digital scarcity (Bitcoin) gains structural value as AI drives abundance in services, software, and information goods
Institutional AI capital monoculture increases the attractiveness of uncorrelated alternative macro trades
trade_ideas: Long Bitcoin as primary macro hedge against AI-driven abundance era
Underweight AI hardware infrastructure relative to Wall Street consensus positioning

entries.summary: John Mauldin's 'G-Shaped Economy' thesis describes a bifurcated recovery where government spending and AI-adjacent sectors thrive while most of the traditional economy stagnates — far more fragile than headline GDP suggests. He warns that federal debt 'will be forcing major changes on the economy,' placing the Fed in a 'no-win situation' where any policy path damages credibility, with CBO's 1.8% real GDP growth assumption masking severe downside risk from potential recessions.
key_views: G-shaped economy: government spending and AI sectors surge while traditional economy stagnates — headline GDP masks underlying bifurcation
Federal debt out of control and will force major structural changes on the economy — CBO's 1.8% real GDP growth is an optimistic baseline
Fed in a 'no-win situation' — any policy path damages credibility; trapped between inflation and growth support
Inflation high + unemployment potentially rising = stagflation risk that consensus is not pricing correctly
Best-case scenario requires modest growth + modest inflation + bipartisan fiscal restraint — politically implausible in current environment
trade_ideas: Short long-duration bonds as fiscal dominance and debt dynamics persist
Long hard assets and inflation hedges as stagflation risk underpriced
Underweight sectors dependent on credit access as rates stay higher for longer

entries.summary: Druckenmiller published a WSJ op-ed on August 24 titled 'Let the Bond Market Speak,' publicly accusing Treasury Secretary Bessent of 'price management' — not liquidity management — after Bessent doubled bond buybacks to $4B as 30-year yields hit a 19-year high. Druckenmiller warned that 'every basis point of artificial yield suppression is a subsidy to procrastination,' that markets will test and overwhelm Bessent's intervention forcing ever-larger Treasury purchases, and that the long-term bond yield is 'the only fiscal disciplinarian the U.S. has left.' His prescription: restrict buybacks to small, scheduled off-the-run operations at quarterly refundings only, and fix the primary deficit directly.
key_views: Bessent's buyback doubling is 'price management, not liquidity management' — every suppressed basis point subsidizes fiscal procrastination
Bond market intervention is self-reinforcing: markets will test Bessent's resolve, forcing ever-larger Treasury purchases
The 30-year Treasury yield is 'the only fiscal disciplinarian the U.S. has left' — suppressing it destroys the fiscal warning signal
Buybacks should be restricted to small, scheduled, off-the-run liquidity operations at quarterly refundings — never off-cycle yield suppression
The only durable fix is addressing the primary deficit directly; manipulating the yield curve only delays the reckoning
trade_ideas: Long 30-year Treasury yields (bearish on Bessent's ability to sustainably suppress them)
Short US fiscal credibility via long-end rate volatility

entries.summary: Bessent doubled Treasury bond buybacks to at least $4B on August 19 — with signals it could go higher — as 30-year yields hit a 19-year high, directly intervening to suppress long-term borrowing costs. He simultaneously declared the K-shaped economy 'is over,' citing 2% real wage gains for the bottom 25% of workers. By August 24, reports emerged that Bessent may tap the near-$1 trillion Treasury General Account to fund further buybacks — a strategy publicly condemned by Druckenmiller as reckless yield curve manipulation that will ultimately be overwhelmed by markets.

Doubled Treasury buybacks to at least $4B on Aug 19 as 30-yr yield hit 19-year high; signaled operations could exceed $4B
Yields 'don't reflect market fundamentals' — Bessent sees weak 30-year liquidity as justification for intervention
Near-$1 trillion Treasury General Account may be tapped as a funding source for expanded buybacks
Faces a structural tension: suppressing yields for fiscal relief while also managing tariff wars and Iran sanctions
trade_ideas: Buying off-the-run long-term Treasuries (10-30yr) via expanded buyback program
Potential TGA drawdown as stealth fiscal stimulus signal

entries.summary: Dalio warns of an approaching debt crisis and textbook AI asset bubble comparable to 1929 and 2000 levels, with >50% chance of 'trauma' if the U.S. budget deficit isn't addressed. He recommends defensive positioning in gold and bitcoin as the global 80-year grand cycle enters its final stage, while identifying significant supply/demand imbalances in bond markets.

AI asset bubble is textbook and reaching 1929/2000 severity levels
U.S. budget deficit poses >50% probability of economic trauma without policy intervention
80-year global grand cycle entering final stage
Bond market facing structural supply/demand problem
Wealth is not the same as money—critical distinction in inflationary environment
trade_ideas: Long gold as crisis hedge
Long bitcoin as crisis hedge and alternative to currency debasement

Short or exit nuclear energy sector positions

Gold positioned to benefit from dollar weakness and Trump pressure on the Fed

He views the AI narrative as riskier than consensus recognizes and flags a 2007-era bond market warning, while suggesting the Bank of Canada should look through tariff-driven inflation to support growth.

entries.summary: Ed Yardeni maintains a bullish stance on equities, citing strong earnings momentum and AI-driven economic stimulus as the primary drivers of the current market rally. He distinguishes the current AI-led rally from the 1999 dot-com bubble by framing it as 'FEMO' (Fundamentals-Driven Emotion) rather than 'FOMO' (Fear of Missing Out), and has raised his 2026 S&P 500 price target to 8,400. He views temporary pullbacks like the June swoon as AI fatigue rather than fundamental market weakness.

His successor at Bridgewater, Greg Jensen, articulates how modern mercantilism and AI are simultaneously driving two accelerating resource grabs — semiconductors and data infrastructure — that reshape how money flows globally. Dalio's overarching thesis of eroding foreign confidence in US assets and a potential policy-induced recession remains his core macro warning for 2026.

Yardeni projects S&P 500 EPS rising from $268 to $310 next year, and views Treasury yields in a 4-5% 'normal range' as non-threatening to the expansion. entries.summary: Napier's February 2026 podcast laid out his financial repression thesis with increased conviction: governments will hold interest rates below the rate of inflation for at least 15 years — just as post-WWII — to inflate away unsustainable debt levels. He forecasts 4-5.5% inflation over the next decade in developed markets while real rates stay deeply negative. Bond yields will no longer be market-determined, and most skills investors learned post-1979 (i.e., since inflation was tamed) are 'obsolete.' entries.summary: Mauldin frames 2026 as a 'Global Restructuring' — not a cyclical recession but a fundamental reorder of geopolitical and economic relationships that will look transformative in hindsight. He describes a 'Bipolar Economy' where boom and bust coexist by sector and region, making traditional macro analysis insufficient. His GeoMacro framework integrates geopolitics from the outset rather than as an afterthought. Under his 'Muddle Through' scenario — 1.3% real GDP, ~3% inflation, ~4.2% unemployment — CBO projects only 1.8% growth through 2035.
key_views: 'Global Restructuring' — 2026 is a reorder, not just a recession; will look transformative in 15 years
'Bipolar Economy': boom and bust sectors coexisting — traditional macro analysis can't capture it
GeoMacro framework essential: geopolitics must be integrated into investment theses from the outset
Muddle Through baseline: 1.3% real GDP, ~3% inflation, 4.2% unemployment — CBO projects 1.8% growth 2026-2035
US-China detente likely: both sides need each other too much economically to let disputes fester
trade_ideas: Diversify globally — Muddle Through scenario favors international over US-centric allocation
Integrate geopolitical risk into every investment thesis from the start

entries.summary: Visser published a specific July 14 CNBC call that consumer AI agents are 'the next big surprise' and that Apple is an unexpected winner — distinct from his earlier broad AI/macro disruption thesis. He argues the agentic AI layer will compress costs and create deflationary pressure in services, while Apple's tight OS/hardware integration positions it to capture consumer agent share from OpenAI. Bottlenecks in AI infrastructure (energy, compute) are shifting market leadership from semiconductor buildout plays to consumer-facing agent deployers.
key_views: Consumer AI agents are 'the next big surprise' — the next major market-moving theme after data center buildout
Apple is an unlikely AI winner: OS+hardware integration creates defensible moat vs OpenAI in consumer agent market
AI infrastructure bottlenecks (energy, compute) shifting leadership from chips/semis to hyperscaler and agent deployers
Humanoids, robotaxis, and AI drug discovery create structural deflationary pressure on services inflation
Market rotation into value, commodities, and international underway as AI capex cycle matures
trade_ideas: Long Apple as consumer AI agent beneficiary
Rotate from semiconductor capex plays toward consumer-facing agent deployers

entries.summary: Rosenberg breaks sharply from the stagflation consensus, arguing inflation will 'crater' by year-end even as oil prices surge on Iran tensions. His thesis: higher oil prices trigger a consumer cost squeeze that slows demand, ultimately sending inflation in reverse. He warns that analysts pricing 19% S&P 500 earnings growth for 2026 require profit margins reaching new record highs on top of already-record levels — structurally impossible with nominal GDP tracking only 4-5%. His latest memo recommends de-risking, moving to cash, and not chasing tail risks.
key_views: Inflation will 'crater' by year-end despite oil price surge — consumer cost squeeze kills demand and reverses prices
Stagflation consensus is wrong: higher oil is ultimately deflationary when consumers are already stretched
19% S&P earnings growth consensus structurally impossible with nominal GDP at 4-5% and margins already at records
H2 2026 economic strain ahead after tax-refund boost fades — significant deceleration likely
Recession probability exceeds renewed boom probability — de-risk, move to cash, avoid chasing tail risks
trade_ideas: De-risk equity exposure, move to cash
Avoid chasing tail risks in current environment

entries.summary: Wilson updated his sector rotation thesis in two Bloomberg notes: a July 6 call for rotating from semiconductors to hyperscalers as chip momentum fades, and a July 13 note showing S&P 1500 median constituent tracking 10%+ EPS growth this quarter — the best earnings breadth since the post-COVID recovery. The bull case is broadening well beyond Mag-7, supporting his year-end S&P 500 target of 7,800. Near-term, a liquidity squeeze (not rate hikes) remains the primary risk to equity momentum.
key_views: Chip momentum fading — rotate from semiconductors to hyperscalers as AI infrastructure spending enters deployment phase
Median S&P 1500 constituent tracking 10%+ EPS growth — best earnings breadth since post-COVID recovery
Bull market broadening is the defining 2026 development: cyclicals, industrials, and financials now contributing alongside tech
S&P 7,800 year-end target intact — multiple expansion for median stock remains underappreciated upside catalyst
Liquidity squeeze (not rate hikes) is primary near-term threat to equity momentum
trade_ideas: Rotate from semiconductor/chip ETFs toward hyperscaler/AI cloud names
Overweight median S&P 1500 vs Mag-7 concentration for earnings breadth trade

entries.summary: BofA's July 14 Global Fund Manager Survey shows investors have swung to their most bullish positioning since February 2026, even as Hartnett's Bull & Bear Indicator remains at a contrarian sell-signal 9.5. Hartnett articulates a 'Four Won'ts' consensus — no hard landing, no Fed hike before midterms, no AI capex cuts, no Democrat midterm sweep — and warns any single leg failing triggers a violent correction. He flags Japan bank stocks as a global 'canary': JGB yields near 3% and Japanese bank stocks tripled over three years, a signal that duration risk is being seriously mispriced elsewhere.
key_views: BofA FMS: investors most bullish since February 2026 — consensus and Bull & Bear at 9.5 sell signal diverging dangerously
'Four Won'ts' consensus — any single failure (hard landing, Fed hike, AI capex cut, Dem sweep) = violent correction
AI bubble = #1 tail risk for 45% of Fund Manager Survey respondents; AI capex at $800B in 2026, $1T in 2027
Japan bank stocks are the global 'canary' — JGB yields near 3%, bank stocks tripled in 3 years, signaling real duration risk
Investors remain 'frozen bullish' despite 5% long-bond yields — positioning not adjusting to yield signal
trade_ideas: 'Sleep like a baby' portfolio: 25% stocks / 25% bonds / 25% cash / 25% commodities

entries.summary: Goldman Sachs forecasts US growth cooling to 'stall speed' of just 1.25-1.75% in H2 2026 after June nonfarm payrolls came in at only 57,000 jobs — well below expectations and a second consecutive weak reading. Hatzius cut the 12-month US recession probability to 15% (from 25%) in June after an Iran peace deal removed the geopolitical risk premium. June CPI printed 3.5% annually, below the 3.8% consensus, as energy prices pulled back — though core services inflation and elevated Fed hawkishness under Kevin Warsh keep any near-term cut off the table.
key_views: US H2 2026 growth: 1.25-1.75% 'stall speed' — minimal buffer above recession territory, a downshift from the H1 2.6% call
June payrolls: only 57,000 jobs — second consecutive miss, labor market weakness becoming 'too entrenched' for cyclical reversal
Recession probability cut to 15% (from 25%) after Iran peace deal removed geopolitical risk premium (June 22)
June CPI: 3.5% vs 3.8% expected — energy pullback provides relief but core services remain sticky
Fed under Warsh: hawkish first meeting, higher-for-longer bias with rate hike back in play before year-end

entries.summary: Schwab's July 2026 Market Snapshot shows the bull market intact with 25% full-year S&P 500 earnings growth consensus, but Sonders highlights deepening fault lines: June CPI at 3.5% (below 3.8% expected) and June payrolls at only 57,000 jobs signal simultaneous slowing labor market and sticky inflation. Renewed US-Iran tensions have driven oil higher, acting as a supply-side shock on consumers already running thin on savings. The Great Moderation era of low volatility is over — Sonders argues the new regime of instability favors flexibility and diversification over passive buy-and-hold.
key_views: Bull market alive with 25% S&P earnings growth consensus but growth dangerously concentrated in tech (Alphabet, Broadcom, Micron, Sandisk, Intel)
June CPI 3.5% vs 3.8% expected — energy pullback provided temporary relief; core services inflation still elevated
June payrolls 57,000 — second consecutive miss; labor market cooling faster than headline GDP suggests
Renewed US-Iran tensions driving oil higher — new supply shock hitting households with low savings rates and weak real wage growth
Great Moderation over: new era of instability favors flexibility and diversification over passive exposure

entries.summary: Druckenmiller argues 'contrarianism is overrated' — staying long US equities while hedging the dollar via commodities and international exposure. He remains AI-centric ('all that matters is AI and Nvidia'), pairing that equity conviction with a structural dollar-bearish stance expressed through copper and a notable South American macro trade (Brazil's R$33B institutional inflow trade). Duquesne is up 9.8% YTD and 28.4% over the past year, with portfolio shifts tilting away from broad domestic growth toward AI-infrastructure and international opportunities.
key_views: 'Contrarianism is overrated' — stay long US equities, don't fight the AI rally
All that matters is AI and Nvidia — tech dominance driving compounding returns
Structurally bearish on the US dollar; long assets that benefit from USD weakness
South American macro trade: Brazil institutional inflow play (R$33B) in natural resources
Copper long as explicit USD hedge alongside commodities
trade_ideas: Long US equities (AI/tech focused)
Long copper as USD hedge
Long Brazil assets (R$33B institutional inflow theme)

entries.summary: Dalio (now managing his family office after fully exiting Bridgewater) continues to warn investors are entering the most dangerous phase of the 'Big Cycle,' citing 500 years of history showing converging debt crises, political disorder, and geopolitical conflict. He frames the 2026 environment as one of 'capital wars' and 'modern mercantilism,' with tariffs potentially creating 1-2% GDP drag alongside 4-5% sticky inflation — a stagflation trap he sees as highly dangerous for the Fed. Dalio advocates diversifying away from US dollar assets toward gold, real assets, and non-US equities.
key_views: 'Most dangerous phase of the Big Cycle' — debt, disorder, and geopolitical conflict converging for first time in 500 years
'Capital wars' replacing globalization — national self-interest and modern mercantilism dominant
Tariff stagflation: 1-2% GDP drag + 4-5% sticky inflation could force Fed into policy trap
AI arms race adds systemic risk on top of already-stressed fiscal/monetary architecture
No longer at Bridgewater; managing permanent family office capital
trade_ideas: Diversify away from US dollar assets — non-US equities and bonds
Long gold and real assets as Big Cycle hedge

entries.summary: Jones said on CNBC (May 7, 2026) that the AI-fueled bull market has 'another year or two to run,' drawing explicit parallels to 1999 — roughly a year before the dot-com peak. He recently bought more AI-related stocks, viewing the AI era similarly to Microsoft's early software dominance and the 1990s internet build-out. However, he warned that when the cycle ends, corrections will be 'breathtaking' if markets go up another 40% first, and he raised concerns about AI's long-term systemic risks requiring government regulation.
key_views: AI bull market has 'another year or two to run' — 1999 parallel, one year before dot-com peak
Bought more AI-related stocks recently — conviction in near-term upside
Warns of 'breathtaking corrections' when AI bubble ends if markets extend another 40%
AI regulation inevitable — long-term systemic/existential risk concerns
AI parallels Microsoft 1980s and internet 1990s — years of productivity gains ahead
trade_ideas: Long AI-related equities with active monitoring for bubble signals
Maintain hedges given 'breathtaking' correction risk at extended levels

entries.summary: Marks's Oaktree 2026 conference highlighted that direct lending has become commoditized, with alpha migrating to more complex strategies: asset-backed finance and distressed credit. His recent AI memo argues AI is unambiguously transformative — 'far from a fad' — but urges investors to weigh that transformational potential against current AI asset valuations, which he views as a critical and underappreciated variable. Marks continues to emphasize exploiting mispricings created by complexity, forced selling, and market misunderstandings rather than relying on efficient market pricing.
key_views: Direct lending alpha has disappeared as capital flooded post-2011 — pivot to asset-backed finance and distressed credit
AI is transformative and 'far from a fad' — immense power, speed, and autonomy vs prior tech waves
AI asset prices must be weighed against transformational potential — valuation discipline essential
Mispricings arise from complexity, forced selling, supply-demand imbalances, and misunderstandings
Superior thinking, not efficient market reliance, is the edge in private credit
trade_ideas: Long asset-backed finance and distressed credit over commoditized direct lending
Selective AI-adjacent equities where valuation supports transformational thesis

entries.summary: Appaloosa Management surged 32% in H1 2026 on memory chip bets, with all gains generated in Q2 (Bloomberg, July 6). Tepper's Q1 2026 13F portfolio shrank to ~$5.93B across 31 highly concentrated positions — top holdings AMZN, MU, GOOGL, UBER, and TSM — reflecting exit of nearly all bank stocks and a 200% increase in Micron as a high-bandwidth memory AI pick-and-shovel play. Despite the strong performance, Tepper maintains an average 40% cash position, signaling conservative risk management amid AI-driven returns.
key_views: Appaloosa up 32% H1 2026 — all gains in Q2, driven by memory chip sector
High-conviction AI memory play: Micron (HBM) as primary AI pick-and-shovel position, increased 200%
Exited nearly all bank stocks in Q4 2025 — structural rotation away from financials
High concentration: AMZN, MU, GOOGL, UBER, TSM as top 5 holdings in $5.93B portfolio
40% average cash position — conservative risk management despite strong performance
trade_ideas: Long Micron (MU) as AI high-bandwidth memory infrastructure play
Long AMZN, GOOGL, TSM, UBER (top concentration)

entries.summary: Gundlach stated in May 2026 that it is 'just not possible' for the Fed to cut rates — and would bet on hikes instead — citing the 2-year Treasury trading ~50bps above the Fed funds rate and persistently sticky inflation. He proposed a specific portfolio architecture: 30% non-US equities, 20% real assets (10% gold, 5% commodities, 5% other), 30% high-quality bonds, and 20% cash. His core macro thesis is 'dollar negative' — non-US equities are the most important structural overweight — paired with gold as the primary real asset anchor.
key_views: 'Just not possible' for Fed to cut rates in 2026 — would bet on rate hikes instead
2Y Treasury ~50bps above Fed funds rate makes cuts unjustifiable; inflation remains sticky
Dollar structurally bearish — non-US equities (30%) as primary overweight
Gold 10% and commodities 5% as real asset anchors against dollar weakness and inflation
30% high-quality bonds + 20% cash as defensive foundation
trade_ideas: Long non-US equities (30% allocation)
Long gold (10%) and commodities (5%) as real asset anchors
Underweight US dollar assets; avoid duration in inflation environment

entries.summary: Burry's Scion Asset Management fully exited China (Alibaba, JD.com, Baidu liquidated in one move — a macro statement) while initiating a new long in MercadoLibre (MELI), marking a return to Latin American e-commerce. He maintains large put options on Nvidia and Palantir, expressing deep AI-valuation skepticism even as the rally continues. The SaaS rotation is his constructive bet: Scion is accumulating beaten-down SaaS names (Adobe, Autodesk, Veeva) targeting low stock-based compensation, strong 'owner earnings,' and AI productivity beneficiaries.
key_views: Full China exit: BABA, JD.com, Baidu all liquidated simultaneously — decisive macro move
AI skeptic: large put options on Nvidia and Palantir against the AI rally
New long: MercadoLibre (MELI) — return to Latin American e-commerce after prior exit
SaaS rotation: Adobe, Autodesk, Veeva as beaten-down AI productivity beneficiaries
Selective bullishness within cautious macro stance — portfolio ~$68M (personal vehicle post-deregistration)
trade_ideas: Long MercadoLibre (MELI)
Long Adobe, Autodesk, Veeva (beaten-down SaaS)
Short Nvidia and Palantir via puts

entries.summary: Brevan Howard's $11.2B BH Master Fund is generating equity-driven gains that are offsetting losses in rates and FX — a structural shift in where macro alpha is found. The firm wound down the $1.4B FG Fund by end-June 2026 and saw Tekmerion Capital spin out with $1B+. Howard is simultaneously expanding the macro trading team and positioning Brevan as a broader alternative manager, with its Brevan Howard Digital unit managing billions in digital assets. The pivot reflects a view that traditional rates/FX macro is less productive while equities and digital assets offer richer opportunities.
key_views: Equity trading gains now offsetting rates/FX losses — macro alpha has migrated from traditional strategies
$1.4B FG Fund closed June 2026 — eliminating less-differentiated strategies
Tekmerion Capital spinout: $1B+ commitment signals talent migration to independent platforms
Expanding macro team despite mixed H1 — conviction in macro opportunity set intact
Digital assets expansion: Brevan Howard Digital managing billions — structural crypto bet
trade_ideas: Equities as primary macro return driver (replacing rates)
Digital assets via dedicated Brevan Howard Digital unit

entries.summary: Treasury Secretary Bessent reiterated his '3-3-3' framework — 3% GDP growth, 3% deficit-to-GDP, and 3M bpd domestic oil production — and predicted GDP with 'a three in front of it' before year-end (CNBC, June 24). He testified to the Senate that the economy remains strong and on track, explicitly rejecting recession fears and calling 2026 a 'blockbuster year.' His broader thesis frames Treasury's role as economic statecraft — directing American capital toward sectors deemed critical to national security and long-term competitiveness.
key_views: 3-3-3 framework: 3% GDP growth, 3% deficit-to-GDP, 3M bpd domestic oil production
GDP growth 'with a three in front of it' achievable before year-end (CNBC, June 24)
No US recession in 2026 — 'blockbuster year' prediction maintained
Economic statecraft: Treasury directing capital toward national-security-critical manufacturing and tech
Iran energy shock will prove transitory; Fed's 2% inflation target achievable
trade_ideas: Long US equities on growth and deregulation narrative
Long domestic energy production (3M bpd increase policy)

entries.summary: Ackman called current conditions 'one of the best times in a long time to buy quality stocks,' arguing that some of the highest-quality businesses in the world are trading at 'stupidly cheap' prices with potential for 10x returns. His macro framework sees inflation as bullish for quality compounders, GDP slowing but not contracting, and rates staying higher for longer — a backdrop he views as creating mispriced opportunities. He characterizes Pershing Square as 'constructive on the current economic and market backdrop,' launched Pershing Square USA in April 2026, and continues to accumulate long-duration quality compounders.
key_views: 'Best time in a long time to buy quality' — some high-quality businesses 'stupidly cheap'
Macro framework: inflation bullish for quality compounders, GDP slowing but not contracting
Higher-for-longer rates creating mispricings in long-duration quality businesses
Pershing Square 'constructive on the current economic and market backdrop'
Pershing Square USA IPO launched April 2026 ($5B) — expanding to retail investors
trade_ideas: Long high-quality compounders trading at discounts (Alphabet, Amazon, Meta cited)
Pershing Square USA provides retail access to Ackman's concentrated quality positions

entries.summary: Einhorn's Greenlight Capital closed to new investors as of July 1, 2026, signaling the firm sees elevated downside risk in US equities — 'the most expensive we've seen since we began managing money and arguably in the history of the United States.' Capital preservation is now Einhorn's top priority, willing to miss upside to be positioned offensively 'should one of the downside scenarios materialize.' All of Greenlight's 2025 alpha came from the macro portfolio (14.4% gross contribution), with notable wins including Lebanese debt at 66% IRR; for 2026 Einhorn prefers direct exposures to gold, copper, and rates over equities.
key_views: US equities 'most expensive we've seen since we began managing money' — historically extreme valuations
Closed to new investors July 1, 2026 — limiting inflows as downside risk elevated
Capital preservation is top priority — willing to miss upside to play more offense on downturn
All 2025 alpha from macro portfolio (14.4% gross): gold, copper, rates, Lebanese debt (66% IRR)
Prefers direct exposure to gold, copper, rates over equity proxies
trade_ideas: Long gold directly
Long copper directly
Long rates (bonds)
Event-driven credit (Lebanese debt restructuring)

entries.summary: Reid published a major note on July 7-8, 2026 warning that AI productivity gains are 'years away' from materializing in economic data, creating a critical debt risk: if AI doesn't deliver on its productivity promise, already-unsustainable global debt levels worsen significantly. He frames this as the central bull/bear divide of 2026: bulls hope AI becomes 'a productivity miracle you can grow into debt'; bears warn that if rates lift much above current levels, debt sustainability becomes problematic. Deutsche Bank's 2026 theme is 'never a dull moment' — volatile boom-bust narrative swings, with Germany's fiscal rebound and China's moderation as key regional divergences.
key_views: AI productivity gains are 'years away' — economic embedding of AI takes time despite immense potential (July 7-8 note)
Debt sustainability risk: if AI underdelivers, unsustainable global debt levels worsen materially
Bull/bear 2026 divide: AI as productivity miracle to grow into debt (bulls) vs rates rise + debt crisis (bears)
2026 theme: 'never a dull moment' — markets will swing sharply between boom-bust narratives
Germany fiscal rebound major; China moderating on anti-involution reforms; Fed 2 more cuts then pause

entries.summary: Slok's mid-year 2026 outlook identifies three forces driving the economy: the AI data center buildout, an industrial renaissance, and the One Big Beautiful Bill fiscal stimulus — together adding ~2.2 percentage points to GDP per CBO estimates. He notes the economy is 'resilient and doing quite well,' but is increasingly worried about overheating rather than stagflation: inflation could start moving up in H2 2026 as capacity tightens. Consumer and business spending both remain strong, and data center financing is already committed, providing multi-quarter AI-capex momentum.
key_views: Three growth forces: AI data center buildout (+1% GDP), industrial renaissance (+0.3%), fiscal stimulus/OBBB (+0.9%)
Risk has shifted from stagflation to OVERHEATING — inflation could move up in H2 2026
Economy 'resilient and doing quite well' — consumer and business spending both strong
Data center financing already committed — AI capex has multi-quarter momentum regardless of sentiment
K-shaped divergence: headline strength masking significant sector and income disparities

entries.summary: Hartnett's Bull & Bear Indicator hit 9.5 for multiple consecutive weeks as of early July 2026 — a contrarian sell signal — while global equity funds attracted $56.6B in the week ending July 8 (4th-largest weekly inflow of 2026). He calls the current AI market the 'largest bubble since the 1880s railroad boom,' with Mag 7 concentration at 48% of S&P 500 exceeding all historical bubble peaks. Japan bank stocks are flagged as the 'canary' for a global sell-off. His post-bubble playbook recommends 25/25/25/25 stocks/bonds/cash/commodities — the best-performing allocation since 1933.
key_views: Bull & Bear Indicator at 9.5 — contrarian sell signal for multiple consecutive weeks
AI market = largest bubble since 1880s railroad boom; Mag 7 at 48% of S&P concentration
$56.6B weekly equity inflows (week ending July 8) — 4th-largest of 2026 despite sell signals
Japan bank stocks = 'canary' — rising JGB yields could trigger global risk sell-off
Post-bubble playbook: 25/25/25/25 stocks/bonds/cash/commodities best since 1933
trade_ideas: Reduce equity concentration; shift toward 25/25/25/25 stocks/bonds/cash/commodities
Monitor Japan bank stocks as early warning for global correction

entries.summary: Edwards has pivoted his long-running 'Ice Age' thesis (secular stagnation, falling bond yields) toward fiscal dominance and the risk of double-digit inflation returning (Bloomberg, May 15, 2026). He argues governments, constrained by electoral pressures, are unable to unwind fiscal expansion, creating unsustainable debt-to-GDP trajectories in the US and UK. The underlying consumer is 'tapped out' — low savings, rising costs — threatening corporate margins even as AI-driven equity gains persist. This is a major evolution: Edwards now warns of an inflationary fiscal-dominance regime, not the deflationary Ice Age he long predicted.
key_views: Ice Age thesis has evolved: fiscal dominance + double-digit inflation risk now the dominant concern (May 2026)
Governments unable to unwind fiscal expansion due to electoral constraints — unsustainable US and UK debt trajectories
Underlying consumer 'tapped out' — low savings and rising costs threatening corporate margins
AI equity gains unsustainable if consumer spending collapses under cost pressures
Regime shift: from deflationary Ice Age to inflationary fiscal dominance — major thesis evolution
trade_ideas: Avoid long-duration bonds — fiscal dominance creates persistent inflation risk premium
Long inflation protection: TIPS, commodities, real assets

entries.summary: Rosenberg frames 2026 as a 'Global Restructuring' — not a mere recession or correction but a fundamental reorder of the kind that looks transformative in 15 years' hindsight. He characterizes the economy as 'Bipolar' — extreme data swings driven by tariff front-running, government shutdowns, and geopolitical shocks — with GDP growth averaging 2.7% YoY through March 2026 but Q4 2025 GDP at just 0.5%. His Rosie Macro Fund is up 28% YTD vs S&P 500 at 14%, validating his contrarian strategy; he expects pronounced disinflation to force the Fed to cut more aggressively than markets currently price.
key_views: 'Global Restructuring' — fundamental 15-year reorder, not a recession; geopolitics redefining economics
'Bipolar Economy' — extreme data swings from tariff front-running, shutdowns, and geopolitical shocks
GDP averaging 2.7% YoY through March 2026, but Q4 2025 GDP only 0.5% (government shutdown impact)
Disinflation will force the Fed to cut more aggressively than currently priced
Rosie Macro Fund up 28% YTD vs S&P 500 +14% — going public as a listed ETF
trade_ideas: Long bonds on disinflation-driven Fed rate-cut narrative
Rosie Macro ETF launching as publicly listed vehicle

entries.summary: Yardeni raised his 2026 S&P 500 target to 8,250 (from 7,700) after a 'gangbusters' Q1 2026 earnings season, saying he 'wasn't bullish enough,' while maintaining his 'Roaring 2020s' thesis and long-term target of 10,000 by decade-end. He projects 3% GDP growth, 2.5% productivity gains, and $310 EPS for 2026, underpinned by the 'BRAIN Revolution' (Biotech, Robotics, AI, Nanotechnology). He expects only one Fed rate cut and views inflation as having peaked in 2025, moderating toward target. He sees 2026 theme as a rotation from AI producers to the 493 S&P companies that benefit from AI cost reduction.
key_views: 'Roaring 2020s' thesis intact — S&P 500 target raised to 8,250 after gangbusters Q1 earnings; 'wasn't bullish enough'
Long-term S&P 500 target: 10,000 by decade-end
BRAIN Revolution driving productivity: Biotech, Robotics, AI, Nanotechnology
2026 rotation: from AI producers to 493 AI user beneficiaries gaining from cost cuts and efficiency
Only 1 Fed rate cut anticipated in 2026; inflation peaked in 2025 and moderating
trade_ideas: Long S&P 500 broad index with 8,250 target
Rotate from AI producers (NVDA, SMCI) to AI user beneficiaries ('493' companies)

entries.summary: Goldman Sachs projects global GDP growth of 2.8% in 2026 (vs 2.5% consensus), with US growth accelerating to 2.6% as tariff headwinds fade and tax cuts kick in. Hatzius expects the Fed to pause in January 2026, then cut in March and June, reaching a terminal rate of 3-3.25%. Regional divergences are key: Germany rebounding strongly on fiscal stimulus, China growing at 4.8% but moderating on anti-involution reforms, euro area at a 'decent' 1.3%. Goldman forecast 'especially strong GDP growth in H1 2026.'
key_views: Global GDP forecast 2.8% (vs 2.5% consensus) — above-trend growth as tariff impact fades
US growth accelerating to 2.6% on tariff fade, tax cuts, and easier financial conditions
Fed: pause January 2026, cut March + June; terminal rate 3-3.25%
Germany: meaningful fiscal-driven rebound; China: 4.8% growth but moderating; euro area: 1.3%
'Especially strong GDP growth' expected in H1 2026

entries.summary: Wilson maintains his 'out-of-consensus' S&P 500 year-end target of 7,800, premised on a new bull cycle that started in April 2025 and is now broadening beyond tech. He projects 17% EPS growth driven by a 'rolling recovery' — manufacturing, housing, and lower-tier consumer goods sectors hitting their troughs at different times and now moving up in sync. This is 'The Bull Market's Underappreciated Narrative': the rally that began in tech is now bleeding into the broader economy, signaling a more inclusive and durable second act to the bull market.
key_views: S&P 500 year-end target 7,800 — 'out-of-consensus' bullish call maintained
New bull cycle started April 2025; entering 'second act' broadening beyond tech
17% EPS growth expected — driven by 'rolling recovery' across lagging sectors
'Rolling recovery': manufacturing, housing, lower-tier consumer hitting troughs and rebounding in sync
Bull market broadening is 'underappreciated narrative' — consensus too focused on tech concentration risk
trade_ideas: Long S&P 500 with sector rotation into manufacturing, housing, consumer discretionary

entries.summary: Napier maintains his thesis that we are entering a 15-20 year period of financial repression — governments structurally keeping interest rates below inflation to inflate away post-pandemic debt, paralleling the post-WWII experience. He argues central banks have become 'irrelevant,' now doing the bidding of indebted sovereigns rather than fighting inflation. Gold is signaling the coming regime shift. Napier warns yield chasing is dangerous and that technology will not defeat inflation; investors should favor real assets over bonds.
key_views: 15-20 year financial repression cycle beginning — structurally elevated inflation, rates kept below it
Central banks 'irrelevant' — now serving indebted sovereigns, no longer independent inflation fighters
Post-WWII parallel: governments will inflate away debt over decades via repression, not austerity
Gold signaling the inflationary regime shift — most reliable leading indicator
Technology will not defeat inflation — productivity gains insufficient vs fiscal dominance pressures
trade_ideas: Long gold as financial repression and inflation-regime hedge
Long real assets broadly; avoid long-duration bonds

entries.summary: Berezin's BCA Research sees 2026 unfolding in two distinct stages: H1 as a 'Great Rotation' from tech stocks to non-tech names, followed by a broad-based selloff in H2 driven by a weakening US economy. US recession probability stands at 40-50%. BCA separately argues that AI will 'kill the tech monopolies' by democratizing capabilities that previously only large platforms could offer, eroding competitive moats. Berezin maintains a structurally bearish view on US equities into H2 despite the early-year tech-to-value rotation thesis.
key_views: 2026 in two stages: H1 'Great Rotation' (tech → non-tech), H2 broad selloff on weakening US economy
US recession probability 40-50% — elevated, weighing on H2 outlook
AI will 'kill the tech monopolies' — democratizing capabilities erodes large-platform competitive moats
Rotate out of tech in H1 ahead of anticipated H2 broad market decline
Bearish structural view on US equities through H2 2026
trade_ideas: Rotate out of tech/Magnificent 7 into non-tech in H1
Reduce overall equity exposure ahead of anticipated H2 selloff

entries.summary: Sonders characterizes the 2026 environment as one of 'instability' rather than mere uncertainty — a distinction she finds important for portfolio construction. GDP growth is likely to stay slightly above the long-term 2-2.5% trend, supported by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's fiscal stimulus skewed toward higher-income consumers and corporations. Inflation is expected to persist near 3%, well above the Fed's 2% target, with fixed income nevertheless offering solid returns as the Fed eventually cuts in response to labor market softening. S&P 500 earnings growth of ~25% is projected for the full year.
key_views: 'Instability' not just uncertainty — current environment demands more defensive portfolio construction
GDP growth slightly above 2-2.5% long-term trend, supported by OBBB fiscal stimulus skewed to higher-income cohorts
Inflation persisting near 3% — significantly above Fed's 2% target despite resilient economy
Fixed income: solid returns expected as Fed eventually cuts on labor market softening
S&P 500 earnings growth ~25% projected for full calendar year 2026
